title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
The aim of this course is to give you the mathematical tools, and enough distance from them, to bring your existing knowledge to bear on the problems that actually arise in insurance. It is not principally a course in actuarial technique. You will meet pricing formulas, risk measures and copulas, and you will be expected to use them correctly by the end, but the recipes are not the point. What the course tries to offer instead is an account of why insurance contracts take the forms they do, why insurers rely on one class of model rather than another, and where common misconceptions about multivariate risk go wrong.
After a historical introduction, intended to put the field at arm’s length for a moment, the argument runs as follows. A risk-averse agent facing an uncertain loss will pay more than the expected loss to be rid of the risk. An insurer able to pool a large number of such risks can accept them for less than each agent would be willing to pay. That gap is the economic basis of the industry. Everything else — the deductible, the premium loading, portfolio segmentation, reinsurance treaties and solvency capital — comes from working out the details under realistic constraints: asymmetric information, dependent losses, limited capital and regulation.
Working out those details requires a mixture of tools, and assembling that mixture is the real mathematical content of the course.

title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
The tools we shall need
Decision theory. Expected utility and risk aversion provide the framework in which we analyse the demand for insurance. The analysis of markets under adverse selection and moral hazard explains much of the form that contracts take, and the trade-off between segmentation and pooling.
Optimisation and the calculus of variations. How much is an agent willing to pay to insure a good, or to transfer a risk? Which form of contract is most desirable? We shall meet optimisation problems on the real line, but also problems posed over spaces of functions, which is where the calculus of variations enters. The well-known result on the optimality of the deductible, for instance, is a variational result.
Probability and statistics. Compound distributions, the collective model, heavy tails, dependence structures, and the asymptotic results that justify pooling — together with the circumstances in which those results fail.

title: Mathematics for Insurance
text:
Prerequisites and expectations
You are expected to be comfortable with probability at the level of a first-year master’s course, with standard results in mathematical statistics, and with constrained optimisation. No prior exposure to insurance is assumed beyond what everyday life provides.
Assessment consists of two written examinations: a mid-term examination and a final examination. Mock examinations will be organised, and past exams are available on Moodle.

Where to go next
The outline sets out the six chapters of the course. The reading list gives the small number of books worth consulting — and, better still, one or two worth reading from cover to cover.

title: Reading
text: No single book covers the whole course. The list below is deliberately short: each title is particularly useful for one or more chapters, and together they provide a good route through most of the material.

title: Reading
text:
Notes on the list
Denuit and Charpentier is the main reference for Chapters 3 to 6 of the course. Volume I, Principes fondamentaux de théorie du risque, covers premium principles, risk measures, stochastic orderings and dependence; Volume II, Tarification et provisionnement, covers generalised linear models, credibility, bonus–malus systems and reserving. The books are written in French and assume little beyond a solid grounding in probability, making them unusually approachable introductions to a technical literature.
Henriet and Rochet is the main reference for Chapter 2. It is short and precise, covering the supply of and demand for insurance, equilibrium under complete information, and then adverse selection and moral hazard. If you read one book alongside the lectures on contract design, make it this one.
Deelstra and Plantin is a concise volume covering premium calculation principles and the institutional reality of the reinsurance market. It is the English-language complement to Chapters 3 and 5 and is particularly useful because it does not separate the mathematics from the market it describes.
Eeckhoudt, Gollier and Schlesinger is a standard modern treatment of decision-making under risk. Read it for the foundations of Chapter 2, and because it connects insurance with the broader field of financial economics.
Borscheid and Haueter is an edited history of the global insurance industry from the late eighteenth century onwards, with chapters devoted to a wide range of countries. It provides useful background reading for Chapter 1. It is a long book, and you are certainly not expected to read it from cover to cover.

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text:
Before studying the demand for insurance, we need a language for comparing risky situations. We shall use the expected-utility framework associated with von Neumann and Morgenstern. The point is not that individuals literally write down a utility function before making a decision; rather, the model gives a coherent mathematical representation of preferences under risk and a convenient language in which to study risk aversion.


Fix a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\). In this section, random variables represent wealth; later, when we focus on insurance, random variables will often represent losses. Let \(\mathcal I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an interval, typically \(\mathbb R\), \(\mathbb R_+=[0,\infty)\) or \(\mathbb R_+^*=(0,\infty)\).
We assume that an agent’s preferences over random wealth levels taking values in \(\mathcal I\) admit an expected-utility representation: there exists a function \(u:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
X \precsim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]\leq \mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
Here \(X\precsim_u Y\) means that the agent weakly prefers \(Y\) to \(X\). Equality defines indifference:
\[
X\sim_u Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb E[u(X)]=\mathbb E[u(Y)].
\]
Throughout this chapter, we restrict attention to random variables for which all the expectations under consideration are well defined and finite. The precise integrability conditions depend jointly on the random variable and on the utility function, and will not be repeated each time.






NoteUtility is not unique



If \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), then \(u\) and
\[
\widetilde u=\alpha u+\beta
\]
represent exactly the same preferences. Any economically meaningful quantity derived from utility should therefore be invariant under positive affine transformations.


We shall assume throughout that \(u\) is continuous on its domain and twice continuously differentiable on the interior of its domain, with
\[
u'(x)>0,
\qquad
u''(x)\leq 0.
\]
The first condition says that more wealth is preferred to less. The second says that the marginal utility of wealth is non-increasing: an additional euro matters less when wealth is already high. The condition \(u''<0\) on the interior of \(\mathcal I\) is a convenient sufficient condition for strict risk aversion; if \(u''(x)=0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\), then \(u\) is affine and increasing (we often normalise it to \(u(x)=x\)), and the agent is risk-neutral.
The geometry of concavity is useful to keep in mind. For \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal I\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
u\bigl(\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\bigr)
\geq
\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1).
\]
The graph of a concave utility function therefore lies above every chord joining two points of the graph.








Figure 1: The utility of an average wealth lies above the corresponding average utility because of concavity.





Concavity has an immediate interpretation under uncertainty.

Theorem 1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(u\) be concave and let \(X\) be an integrable random variable such that \(u(X)\) is integrable. Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u\bigl(\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, meaning that \(X\) is not almost surely constant, the inequality is strict.

Since \(u\) is increasing, Jensen’s inequality means that a risk-averse agent weakly prefers the sure amount \(\mathbb E[X]\) to the random wealth \(X\):
\[
X\precsim_u \mathbb E[X].
\]
A simple classroom example makes the point. Consider the choice between a sure €1 and a fair coin toss paying €0 or €2. At such small stakes, many people are close to indifferent. Multiply all amounts by 10,000 and the reaction is usually quite different: the sure €10,000 is overwhelmingly preferred to a fair gamble between €0 and €20,000. At still larger stakes the effect becomes even clearer. Faced, for instance, with a sure €250,000 rather than a fair gamble between €0 and €1,000,000, virtually everyone in a typical classroom chooses the sure amount, even though it is only half the expected payoff of the gamble.



The previous example suggests a natural way of attaching a monetary value to a risky prospect.

Definition 1 (Certainty equivalent) Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal I\) and assume that \(u(X)\) is integrable. The certainty equivalent of \(X\) for utility \(u\) is the unique sure wealth level \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\in\mathcal I\) satisfying
\[
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr)
=
\mathbb E[u(X)].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(X)]\right).
\]
In French, the same object is the équivalent certain, often denoted \(ec_u(X)\).

The certainty equivalent is a monetary valuation of final wealth: it is the sure wealth level that makes the agent indifferent to the risky wealth \(X\).






NoteCertainty equivalents and indifference prices



When the random variable represents an incremental payoff rather than final wealth, it is often more natural to speak of an indifference price.
Suppose an agent has initial wealth \(w\) and considers buying a risky payoff \(Y\) for a price \(p\). The buyer’s indifference price \(p_u(w,Y)\) is defined, when it exists, by
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w+Y-p_u(w,Y)\bigr)\right]
=
u(w).
\]
It is the maximum price that leaves the agent indifferent between buying the gamble and keeping the initial wealth for certain. In general, this price depends on the background wealth \(w\). It should therefore not be confused with \(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y)\). Under CARA utility (see below) on \(\mathbb R\), however, translation invariance removes the wealth effect and one obtains exactly
\[
p_u(w,Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y).
\]



Proposition 1 (Certainty equivalent and the mean) Let \(u\) be increasing and concave. Whenever the quantities are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u(\mathbb E[X]).
\]
By definition,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is strictly increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to mean wealth, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox is an early illustration of why expected monetary value is not enough to describe choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in correspondence in 1713. A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears; if this occurs on toss \(n\), the payoff is \(2^n\). The expected monetary payoff is infinite, since every possible stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly. His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern. See Bernoulli (1738/1954).





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal I\). Assume that \(u\) is twice continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of \(\mu\), with \(u'(\mu)>0\), and that \(Z\) is bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. A second-order Taylor expansion of \(u\) at \(\mu\) gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u(\mu)
+
u'(\mu)\varepsilon Z
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2Z^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
where boundedness of \(Z\) makes the remainder uniform for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z^2]=1\),
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
Since \(u'(\mu)>0\), the inverse function theorem gives
\[
\bigl(u^{-1}\bigr)'(u(\mu))
=
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}.
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}.
\]
For \(x>0\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and increasing, \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is constant absolute risk aversion (CARA).

Proposition 3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose \(u'>0\) and
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\) in an interval, where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant. Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to a positive affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad C>0.
\]
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad B>0,
\]
which is equivalent under a positive affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\). If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals because willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. It is nevertheless extremely convenient. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the small-risk approximation is not an approximation at all.

Proposition 4 (CARA utility and Gaussian wealth) Let
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
and let
\[
X=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]

The calculation uses the Laplace transform of a standard Gaussian, or equivalently its moment-generating function:
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]

Proof. Since
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\varepsilon Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma_u\equiv\gamma\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\varepsilon^2\), the above second-order formula is exact in this Gaussian/CARA case.







NoteTwo proofs of the Gaussian Laplace transform





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiating under the expectation,
\[
M'(t)
=
\mathbb E[Ze^{tZ}].
\]
Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[
\mathbb E[Zf(Z)]
=
\mathbb E[f'(Z)].
\]
With \(f(z)=e^{tz}\),
\[
M'(t)
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. We say that utility has

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)<0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\);
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)>0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\).

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Some empirical work finds absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, Guiso and Paiella (2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in Cohen and Einav (2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion.

Proposition 5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\qquad
\rho>0.
\]
Then, up to a positive affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion.


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\qquad C>0.
\]
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\). Positive affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

CRRA utility is DARA because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. This restriction is often too rigid empirically. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify or draw an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility \(u\) and another represented by utility \(v\). The key mathematical idea is concavification: one agent is more risk-averse than the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be twice continuously differentiable, strictly increasing utility functions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is strictly increasing, it is invertible on its range. Define
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
This proves both directions.

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\), they assign a lower certainty equivalent to every risky prospect.

Proof. By Proposition 6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

Throughout this chapter, we restrict attention to random variables for which all the expectations under consideration are well defined and finite. The precise integrability conditions depend jointly on the random variable and on the utility function, and will not be repeated each time.






NoteUtility is not unique



If \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), then \(u\) and
\[
\widetilde u=\alpha u+\beta
\]
represent exactly the same preferences. Any economically meaningful quantity derived from utility should therefore be invariant under positive affine transformations.


We shall assume throughout that \(u\) is continuous on its domain and twice continuously differentiable on the interior of its domain, with
\[
u'(x)>0,
\qquad
u''(x)\leq 0.
\]
The first condition says that more wealth is preferred to less. The second says that the marginal utility of wealth is non-increasing: an additional euro matters less when wealth is already high. The condition \(u''<0\) on the interior of \(\mathcal I\) is a convenient sufficient condition for strict risk aversion; if \(u''(x)=0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\), then \(u\) is affine and increasing (we often normalise it to \(u(x)=x\)), and the agent is risk-neutral.
The geometry of concavity is useful to keep in mind. For \(x_0,x_1\in\mathcal I\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
u\bigl(\theta x_0+(1-\theta)x_1\bigr)
\geq
\theta u(x_0)+(1-\theta)u(x_1).
\]
The graph of a concave utility function therefore lies above every chord joining two points of the graph.








Figure 1: The utility of an average wealth lies above the corresponding average utility because of concavity.





Concavity has an immediate interpretation under uncertainty.

Theorem 1 (Jensen’s inequality) Let \(u\) be concave and let \(X\) be an integrable random variable such that \(u(X)\) is integrable. Then
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u\bigl(\mathbb E[X]\bigr).
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, meaning that \(X\) is not almost surely constant, the inequality is strict.

Since \(u\) is increasing, Jensen’s inequality means that a risk-averse agent weakly prefers the sure amount \(\mathbb E[X]\) to the random wealth \(X\):
\[
X\precsim_u \mathbb E[X].
\]
A simple classroom example makes the point. Consider the choice between a sure €1 and a fair coin toss paying €0 or €2. At such small stakes, many people are close to indifferent. Multiply all amounts by 10,000 and the reaction is usually quite different: the sure €10,000 is overwhelmingly preferred to a fair gamble between €0 and €20,000. At still larger stakes the effect becomes even clearer. Faced, for instance, with a sure €250,000 rather than a fair gamble between €0 and €1,000,000, virtually everyone in a typical classroom chooses the sure amount, even though it is only half the expected payoff of the gamble.



The previous example suggests a natural way of attaching a monetary value to a risky prospect.

Definition 1 (Certainty equivalent) Let \(X\) take values in \(\mathcal I\) and assume that \(u(X)\) is integrable. The certainty equivalent of \(X\) for utility \(u\) is the unique sure wealth level \(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\in\mathcal I\) satisfying
\[
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr)
=
\mathbb E[u(X)].
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(\mathbb E[u(X)]\right).
\]
In French, the same object is the équivalent certain, often denoted \(ec_u(X)\).

The certainty equivalent is a monetary valuation of final wealth: it is the sure wealth level that makes the agent indifferent to the risky wealth \(X\).






NoteCertainty equivalents and indifference prices



When the random variable represents an incremental payoff rather than final wealth, it is often more natural to speak of an indifference price.
Suppose an agent has initial wealth \(w\) and considers buying a risky payoff \(Y\) for a price \(p\). The buyer’s indifference price \(p_u(w,Y)\) is defined, when it exists, by
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[u\bigl(w+Y-p_u(w,Y)\bigr)\right]
=
u(w).
\]
It is the maximum price that leaves the agent indifferent between buying the gamble and keeping the initial wealth for certain. In general, this price depends on the background wealth \(w\). It should therefore not be confused with \(\operatorname{ce}_u(Y)\). Under CARA utility (see below) on \(\mathbb R\), however, translation invariance removes the wealth effect and one obtains exactly
\[
p_u(w,Y)=\operatorname{ce}_u(Y).
\]



Proposition 1 (Certainty equivalent and the mean) Let \(u\) be increasing and concave. Whenever the quantities are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
If \(u\) is strictly concave and \(X\) is non-degenerate, the inequality is strict.


Proof. By Jensen’s inequality,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
u(\mathbb E[X]).
\]
By definition,
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is strictly increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\mathbb E[X].
\]
Strict concavity and non-degeneracy give the strict version through the strict form of Jensen’s inequality.

The difference
\[
\pi_u(X)
:=
\mathbb E[X]-\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\geq0
\]
is called the risk premium. It is the discount, relative to mean wealth, associated with bearing the risk.






NoteThe St Petersburg paradox



The St Petersburg paradox is an early illustration of why expected monetary value is not enough to describe choices under risk. Nicolas Bernoulli posed the problem in correspondence in 1713. A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears; if this occurs on toss \(n\), the payoff is \(2^n\). The expected monetary payoff is infinite, since every possible stopping time contributes the same positive amount to the expectation. Yet the fact that the expected payoff is infinite does not make an arbitrarily large entry fee attractive.
Daniel Bernoulli’s celebrated 1738 response was to value wealth through a concave utility function rather than to maximise expected money directly. His central example was logarithmic utility. The episode is historically important because it makes the distinction between money and the utility of money explicit, long before the axiomatic formulation of expected utility by von Neumann and Morgenstern. See Bernoulli (1738/1954).





The certainty equivalent depends both on the distribution of the risk and on the agent’s utility function. For a small risk, these two effects separate particularly cleanly.
Let
\[
X_\varepsilon=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\]
where
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Thus \(\mu\) is the mean wealth and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^2.
\]

Proposition 2 (Certainty equivalent of a small centred risk) Let \(\mu\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal I\). Assume that \(u\) is twice continuously differentiable in a neighbourhood of \(\mu\), with \(u'(\mu)>0\), and that \(Z\) is bounded with
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[Z^2]=1.
\]
Then, as \(\varepsilon\to0\),
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac12\frac{u''(\mu)}{u'(\mu)}\,\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]


Proof. A second-order Taylor expansion of \(u\) at \(\mu\) gives
\[
u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u(\mu)
+
u'(\mu)\varepsilon Z
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2Z^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
where boundedness of \(Z\) makes the remainder uniform for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb E[Z]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[Z^2]=1\),
\[
\mathbb E[u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)]
=
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
u^{-1}\!\left(
u(\mu)
+
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right).
\]
Since \(u'(\mu)>0\), the inverse function theorem gives
\[
\bigl(u^{-1}\bigr)'(u(\mu))
=
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}.
\]
A first-order expansion of \(u^{-1}\) at \(u(\mu)\) therefore yields
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
+
\frac{1}{u'(\mu)}
\left(
\frac12u''(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2)
\right),
\]
which is the stated result.

The expansion separates two ingredients. The amount of risk is represented by the variance \(\varepsilon^2\), while the local attitude towards risk is captured by the curvature ratio evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).
This motivates the fundamental definition.

Definition 2 (Risk aversion coefficients) The coefficient of absolute risk aversion is
\[
\gamma_u(x)
:=
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}.
\]
For \(x>0\), the corresponding coefficient of relative risk aversion is
\[
\rho_u(x)
:=
x\,\gamma_u(x).
\]

The coefficient is classically associated with the work of Arrow and Pratt (1964).
Because \(u\) is concave and increasing, \(\gamma_u(x)\geq0\). More importantly, \(\gamma_u\) is unchanged when \(u\) is replaced by \(\alpha u+\beta\) with \(\alpha>0\): it therefore depends on preferences, not on the arbitrary choice of a utility representation.
With this notation, Proposition 2 becomes
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\mu
-
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2),
\]
or, equivalently,
\[
\pi_u(\mu+\varepsilon Z)
=
\frac12\gamma_u(\mu)\varepsilon^2
+
o(\varepsilon^2).
\]
The leading-order cost of a small risk is therefore the product of a risk term, its variance, and a preference term, the coefficient of absolute risk aversion evaluated at the mean wealth \(\mu\).



A particularly tractable case is constant absolute risk aversion (CARA).

Proposition 3 (Characterisation of CARA utility) Suppose \(u'>0\) and
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\gamma
\]
for every \(x\) in an interval, where \(\gamma\geq0\) is constant. Then:

if \(\gamma=0\), \(u\) is affine and the agent is risk-neutral;
if \(\gamma>0\), then, up to a positive affine transformation,

\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}.
\]
Conversely, \(u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x}\) has constant absolute risk aversion equal to \(\gamma\).


Proof. The equation \(\gamma_u(x)=\gamma\) is
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\gamma,
\]
or equivalently
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\gamma.
\]
Hence
\[
u'(x)
=
C e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad C>0.
\]
If \(\gamma>0\), integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A-B e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad B>0,
\]
which is equivalent under a positive affine transformation to \(-e^{-\gamma x}\). If \(\gamma=0\), then \(u'\) is constant and \(u\) is affine.

CARA is a strong assumption for individuals because willingness to bear a fixed monetary risk does not depend on wealth. It is nevertheless extremely convenient. In particular, for
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
-\frac1\gamma
\log\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma X}],
\]
whenever the expectation is finite, and
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X+c)
=
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)+c.
\]
This translation invariance is one reason CARA specifications are common in models of firms or delegated decision-makers when one wants to analyse profit risk without modelling wealth effects explicitly.
For Gaussian risks the small-risk approximation is not an approximation at all.

Proposition 4 (CARA utility and Gaussian wealth) Let
\[
u(x)=-e^{-\gamma x},
\qquad \gamma>0,
\]
and let
\[
X=\mu+\varepsilon Z,
\qquad
Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]

The calculation uses the Laplace transform of a standard Gaussian, or equivalently its moment-generating function:
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]

Proof. Since
\[
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]
=
e^{t^2/2},
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
-e^{-\gamma\mu}
\mathbb E[e^{-\gamma\varepsilon Z}]
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent,
\[
-e^{-\gamma\operatorname{ce}_u(X)}
=
-\exp\!\left(
-\gamma\mu
+
\frac12\gamma^2\varepsilon^2
\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
=
\mu-\frac12\gamma\varepsilon^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma_u\equiv\gamma\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\varepsilon^2\), the above second-order formula is exact in this Gaussian/CARA case.







NoteTwo proofs of the Gaussian Laplace transform





Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and define
\[
M(t)
=
\mathbb E[e^{tZ}].
\]
We show that
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]
1. Completing the square. Using the Gaussian density,
\[
M(t)
=
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
\exp\!\left(
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
\right)\,dz.
\]
Since
\[
tz-\frac{z^2}{2}
=
-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}
+
\frac{t^2}{2},
\]
we obtain
\[
M(t)
=
e^{t^2/2}
\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\int_{\mathbb R}
e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,dz
=
e^{t^2/2}.
\]
2. A differential equation. Differentiating under the expectation,
\[
M'(t)
=
\mathbb E[Ze^{tZ}].
\]
Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[
\mathbb E[Zf(Z)]
=
\mathbb E[f'(Z)].
\]
With \(f(z)=e^{tz}\),
\[
M'(t)
=
tM(t).
\]
Together with \(M(0)=1\), this differential equation has the unique solution
\[
M(t)=e^{t^2/2}.
\]






Absolute risk aversion need not be constant. We say that utility has

DARA (decreasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)<0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\);
IARA (increasing absolute risk aversion) if \(\gamma_u'(x)>0\) for all \(x \in \mathcal I\).

For individual decision-making, DARA is often regarded as more plausible than CARA: as wealth increases, a fixed monetary gamble becomes less important relative to the agent’s resources. Some empirical work finds absolute risk aversion decreasing with wealth, but the evidence is not uniform and estimated risk attitudes vary substantially across people and elicitation methods. DARA is therefore best viewed as an economically useful benchmark rather than as a universal empirical law; see, for example, Guiso and Paiella (2008) and the rather different insurance-choice evidence in Cohen and Einav (2007).
A second classical family imposes constant relative rather than absolute risk aversion.

Proposition 5 (Characterisation of CRRA utility) Let the domain be \((0,\infty)\) and suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\qquad
\rho>0.
\]
Then, up to a positive affine transformation,
\[
u(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho},
& \rho\neq1,\\[1.1ex]
\log x,
& \rho=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Conversely, these utility functions satisfy
\[
\rho_u(x)
=
x\gamma_u(x)
=
\rho,
\]
and therefore have constant relative risk aversion.


Proof. The equation
\[
\gamma_u(x)
=
\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
gives
\[
-\frac{u''(x)}{u'(x)}
=
\frac{\rho}{x},
\]
hence
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\log u'(x)
=
-\frac{\rho}{x}.
\]
Integrating,
\[
u'(x)
=
C x^{-\rho},
\qquad C>0.
\]
A second integration gives
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\frac{x^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}
\]
when \(\rho\neq1\), and
\[
u(x)
=
A+B\log x
\]
when \(\rho=1\), with \(B>0\). Positive affine transformations remove the irrelevant constants.

CRRA utility is DARA because
\[
\gamma_u(x)=\frac{\rho}{x}
\]
decreases with wealth. It also imposes a very specific rate of decline: doubling wealth halves absolute risk aversion. This restriction is often too rigid empirically. The logarithmic case \(\rho=1\) is the specification associated with Daniel Bernoulli’s classical discussion of the St Petersburg paradox.



People can often answer questions about certainty equivalents – what sure amount would make you indifferent to this lottery? – much more readily than they can specify or draw an entire utility function. It is therefore useful to have a way of comparing the risk aversion of two agents without assigning cardinal meaning to the vertical scales of their utility functions.
Consider one agent represented by utility \(u\) and another represented by utility \(v\). The key mathematical idea is concavification: one agent is more risk-averse than the other precisely when their utility can be obtained from the other’s by applying an additional increasing concave transformation.

Proposition 6 (Comparison of risk aversion) Let \(u\) and \(v\) be twice continuously differentiable, strictly increasing utility functions on the same interval \(\mathcal I\). Then the following statements are equivalent:

for every \(x\in\mathcal I\),
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x);
\]
there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) on \(v(\mathcal I)\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]


In words, the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\) exactly when \(u\) is an increasing concave transformation of \(v\).

Proof. Because \(v\) is strictly increasing, it is invertible on its range. Define
\[
g
:=
u\circ v^{-1}.
\]
Then \(u=g\circ v\), and \(g\) is increasing because both \(u\) and \(v^{-1}\) are increasing. Differentiating the identity
\[
g(v(x))
=
u(x)
\]
gives
\[
g'(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{v'(x)}
>
0.
\]
Differentiating once more,
\[
g''(v(x))
=
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\left(
\gamma_v(x)-\gamma_u(x)
\right).
\]
The factor
\[
\frac{u'(x)}{[v'(x)]^2}
\]
is positive. Hence
\[
g''\leq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\gamma_u\geq\gamma_v.
\]
This proves both directions.

The comparison has an immediate implication for certainty equivalents.

Proposition 7 (Ordering of certainty equivalents) Suppose
\[
\gamma_u(x)
\geq
\gamma_v(x)
\]
for every \(x\in\mathcal I\). Then, for every random variable \(X\) for which the certainty equivalents are well defined,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

Thus, when the agent represented by \(u\) is more risk-averse than the agent represented by \(v\), they assign a lower certainty equivalent to every risky prospect.

Proof. By Proposition 6, there exists an increasing concave function \(g\) such that
\[
u=g\circ v.
\]
Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
\mathbb E[g(v(X))]
\leq
g\bigl(\mathbb E[v(X)]\bigr).
\]
By definition of the certainty equivalent under \(v\),
\[
\mathbb E[v(X)]
=
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
\leq
g\!\left(
v\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr)
\right)
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_v(X)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\mathbb E[u(X)]
=
u\bigl(\operatorname{ce}_u(X)\bigr).
\]
Since \(u\) is increasing,
\[
\operatorname{ce}_u(X)
\leq
\operatorname{ce}_v(X).
\]

title: Microeconomics of insurance
text: Demand for insurance

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



This chapter is intended to provide historical context and general background for the mathematics that follows. It will not be examined: no examination question will require dates, names or historical details from this chapter.
Insurance is much older than the mathematics now used to study it. Communities shared losses, merchants transferred maritime risks and underwriters priced uncertain events long before probability had a formal language. The chronology is useful to keep in mind: institutions usually emerged because people faced concrete risks; mathematics was then introduced, sometimes much later, to understand, price and manage those risks more systematically.
This is necessarily a selective history. The aim is not to identify a single birthplace of insurance, but to follow a few ideas that recur throughout the course: solidarity, pooling, risk transfer, information, diversification, reinsurance and the gradual use of probability and statistics.
Insurance also has a simple economic interpretation. It reallocates purchasing power across possible future states: the policyholder pays a premium in every state and receives an indemnity in some adverse states. The transaction does not create physical resources, and premiums must also finance expenses and capital. It can nevertheless increase welfare for a risk-averse policyholder because money is especially valuable after a loss. We return to this point in Chapter 2.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Before formal insurance: reciprocity and solidarity
text:
Before formal insurance: reciprocity and solidarity
Exchange does not require an anonymous market or immediate monetary settlement. Within families, villages and other communities in which people know one another and expect to interact again, goods and services can circulate through reciprocity, gifts and informal credit. Anthropological work therefore gives little support to a universal sequence in which societies first relied on barter and only later discovered money and credit (Humphrey 1985).
David Graeber popularised the argument that barter was probably not the normal precursor of money within small communities. Where people knew one another and interacted repeatedly, exchange could instead rest on informal credit, reciprocity and obligations carried over time; barter was more characteristic of exchanges with strangers or people unlikely to meet again (Graeber 2011). Graeber’s much broader historical narrative about debt and the origins of money is more controversial, however, and has been criticised on both empirical and interpretative grounds (Maurer 2013). The modest point needed here is much less contentious: repeated relationships allow obligations to be carried through time. Where people know one another, not every exchange has to be settled immediately.
Risk sharing can operate in the same way. A person or household struck by illness, fire, crop failure or death may be helped by relatives, neighbours or a wider community. There is no explicit premium and no calculation of an expected loss, but part of the shock is borne collectively. Informal solidarity is not insurance in the contractual sense, yet it provides an important conceptual precursor: losses that are severe for one person or household can be made more bearable when shared by many.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Antiquity: pooling and maritime risk
The ancient world gives more organised examples. Roman voluntary associations could combine religious, social and occupational functions, including assistance with funerals. Some collected contributions and used common funds to help members meet burial costs (Verboven 2019; Sakaguchi 2002). It would be anachronistic to call these associations insurance companies, but the pooling mechanism is familiar.
Long-distance trade created another problem: a voyage required substantial capital, yet shipwreck, piracy or seizure could destroy the venture. In the Greek maritime loan (nautikon daneion) and its Roman successor, the nauticum foenus, repayment depended on the successful completion of the voyage. Under the agreed conditions, the lender could lose the capital if the ship or cargo was lost (Ste. Croix 1974; Millett 1991).
Such contracts combined two functions that we now usually separate: financing the voyage and bearing part of its risk. The higher return in the successful state compensated the lender both for supplying capital and for accepting the possibility of losing it. Risk transfer was already present, but embedded inside a credit transaction.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Commercial risk sharing across wide trading networks
text:
Commercial risk sharing across wide trading networks
From the early Islamic centuries onwards, commercial networks connected the Mediterranean, Red Sea and Persian Gulf with the Indian Ocean, East Africa, India and South-East Asia. Merchants used partnerships, agency arrangements and credit instruments to mobilise capital across long distances (Udovitch 1970; Chaudhuri 1985).
An important family of contracts was the qirāḍ or muḍāraba: capital was supplied by one party and commercial activity undertaken by another, with profits shared according to an agreed rule and commercial losses normally borne by the invested capital, absent misconduct by the agent (Udovitch 1970). These arrangements were not insurance policies. They are relevant because they show sophisticated ways of allocating capital and commercial risk within legal traditions in which ribā was an important consideration.
European merchants also used partnerships, maritime loans and the commenda to finance trade and distribute risk. Legal restrictions on usury formed part of the environment in which these arrangements developed. The histories are distinct, but the practical questions were similar across trading regions: who supplies the capital, who manages the venture and who bears the loss if it fails?

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Fourteenth-century Italian cities: risk transfer becomes a separate contract
text:
Fourteenth-century Italian cities: risk transfer becomes a separate contract
A major institutional step is visible in the commercial cities of fourteenth-century Italy, especially Genoa and Florence (Balard 1978; Piccinno 2016; Leonard 2016). Maritime risk sharing was not new. What changed was that risk transfer could be separated from the financing of the voyage.
A merchant who already owned a cargo could pay a premium to another party in return for compensation if specified maritime losses occurred. The insurer did not have to lend the merchant the value of the cargo. By the middle of the fourteenth century, surviving contracts contain the essential elements of recognisable marine insurance: a premium, specified risks, an amount exposed to loss and parties willing to bear that loss. The well-known Santa Clara contract from the 1340s is a useful example from this period (Botticini et al. 2023).
Risks could be divided among several underwriters. This limited each participant’s exposure and made information valuable: route, season, vessel, captain, cargo, piracy and war could all affect the price. Premiums were not produced by an actuarial formula. They came from experience, bargaining, reputation and what we would now describe as subjective assessments of risk.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: The Low Countries and Lloyd’s: markets for risk and information
text:
The Low Countries and Lloyd’s: markets for risk and information
As European commerce expanded northwards, Antwerp and then Amsterdam became major centres of marine insurance. In 1598 Amsterdam created the Chamber of Insurance and Average, a specialised institution for disputes involving marine insurance and average (Go 2013). This illustrates an important point: an insurance market needs more than people willing to take risks. It also needs enforceable contracts, brokers, conventions, reputation and mechanisms for resolving disagreements.
London later developed another influential market around Edward Lloyd’s coffee house. The first surviving public reference dates from 1688. Merchants, shipowners, captains, brokers and underwriters gathered there, and the coffee house became particularly valuable as a source of shipping intelligence (Lloyd’s, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). Risks could be shared among several subscribers rather than placed with a single balance sheet. Lloyd’s was therefore not initially an insurance company in the usual sense but a marketplace linking information, brokers and individual risk bearers.
The expansion of insurance accompanied the expansion of long-distance commerce. This is economically natural: transferring risk can make costly and uncertain ventures easier to finance. Insurance itself does not determine whether the activity being facilitated is socially desirable.






CautionHistorical note — insurance and slavery



Marine insurance was also part of the Atlantic slave economy. Underwriters, including participants in the Lloyd’s market, insured ships and commercial interests connected with the trade in enslaved people (Pearson and Richardson 2019; Draper, n.d.). This should be a reminder that a useful mechanism for transferring risk can also support activities that are morally abhorrent.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Fire insurance: pooling and prevention
The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed more than 13,000 houses and demonstrated the scale of correlated urban fire losses (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-b). Commercial fire insurance expanded in the following decades; Nicholas Barbon’s Fire Office was established in 1680 (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-a).
Insured buildings often displayed metal fire marks, and insurers maintained firefighting teams. These brigades had an obvious incentive to limit the spread of fire: an unchecked blaze could damage many insured properties at once. Contrary to a popular story, there is little evidence that insurance brigades routinely allowed uninsured or rival-insured buildings to burn; cooperation was often in their common interest (London Fire Brigade, n.d.-a).
Early fire insurance already displays several recurring themes of non-life insurance: pooling many exposures, classifying risks, recognising accumulation and investing in prevention as well as compensation.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Life assurance and the actuarial turn
text:
Life assurance and the actuarial turn
Life assurance is not the subject of the rest of this course, but it is historically important because life-contingent payments became one of the first areas in which probabilistic calculation was used systematically. Life assurance existed before such pricing. The Amicable Society, founded in London in 1706, operated a genuine life-assurance pool without initially charging age-specific premiums derived from mortality tables (Ogborn 1962).
The intellectual ingredients accumulated gradually. John Graunt’s analysis of the London Bills of Mortality in 1662 was a landmark in quantitative demography (Graunt 1662; Sutherland 2005). Edmond Halley used mortality data from Breslau in 1693 to construct a life table and calculate values for life annuities (Halley 1693). Abraham de Moivre developed methods for life-contingent calculations, and James Dodson later argued for premiums that varied systematically with age.
The Society for Equitable Assurances on Lives and Survivorships, founded in 1762, became an important landmark in long-term life assurance based on age-dependent premiums and mathematical valuation. Richard Price and William Morgan subsequently helped institutionalise regular actuarial valuation (Ogborn 1962; Society of Actuaries, n.d.). The broad lesson is simple: life assurance came first; mortality statistics and probability then changed how it could be priced and managed.






NoteA related instrument: the tontine



Tontines sit between public finance, annuities and longevity risk rather than ordinary indemnity insurance. In the schemes associated with Lorenzo Tonti in the seventeenth century, payments became concentrated among surviving participants. They are worth remembering as another early attempt to organise financial contracts around uncertain lifetimes (Hellwege 2018).

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Industrialisation, reinsurance and the state
The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries created larger concentrations of capital in factories, warehouses, railways, steamships and dense cities. Insurance became part of the infrastructure of industrial investment. Fire insurers gathered information on construction and industrial processes and increasingly differentiated premiums according to observable characteristics (Pearson 2004). New lines of business appeared as technology and liability changed: accident, engineering and employers’ liability were later joined by motor, aviation and many others (Borscheid and Haueter 2012).
Large accumulations of risk also made the limits of a single insurer more obvious. Reinsurance allows an insurer to pass part of its own exposure to another risk bearer. The Hamburg fire of 1842 helped stimulate the creation of Cologne Re in 1846, the first independent professional reinsurance company; the Glarus fire of 1861 was an important background to the foundation of Swiss Re in 1863 (Borscheid et al. 2013; Swiss Re, n.d.). The basic architecture remains with us: households and firms transfer risk to insurers, and insurers transfer part of that risk to reinsurers and capital markets.
Industrialisation and wage labour also changed the political treatment of risk. Germany under Bismarck is a major landmark: legislation in the 1880s introduced compulsory schemes for sickness, industrial accidents, invalidity and old age (Hennock 2007). During the twentieth century, welfare states expanded social insurance and governments increasingly required some private cover, notably motor third-party liability.
The state consequently appears in several roles: regulator, provider of social insurance, purchaser of insurance, authority making some cover compulsory and, for exceptional risks, backstop or reinsurer of last resort. Catastrophes and other highly correlated losses often make the boundary between private and public risk bearing particularly visible.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
section: Probability: theory arrives, then insurance makes use of it
text:
Probability: theory arrives, then insurance makes use of it
For most of the history above, underwriters worked without a formal mathematical theory of probability. That did not mean they ignored uncertainty. They compared routes and vessels, observed claims, negotiated prices and diversified. Their judgements were probabilistic in spirit, but based primarily on experience and market information.
The mathematical calculus of probability initially developed largely elsewhere. Pascal and Fermat’s correspondence in 1654 arose from games of chance; Huygens systematised expectation in 1657. Jacob Bernoulli’s Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, contained the first proof of a law of large numbers (Mattmüller 2014). Pooling, however, did not wait for Bernoulli. The theorem provided a mathematical explanation for a stabilising effect that mutual groups and insurers could already observe in practice.
During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, de Moivre and Laplace developed normal approximations and limit arguments that became part of the history of the central limit theorem (Hald 1990, 1998). Much later, probability was placed on increasingly formal foundations. Borel helped bring probability into the emerging language of measure and integration in France, while the Russian school made major contributions through figures such as Chebyshev, Markov, Khinchin and ultimately Kolmogorov. Kolmogorov’s 1933 axioms gave probability the measure-theoretic framework still used today (Cléry and Mazliak 2022; Kolmogorov 1933; Plato 2005).
This history matters because actuarial practice and probability theory should not be confused. Insurance existed before probability theory, and the foundations of probability were not developed simply in order to solve insurance problems. The two histories eventually met and strongly influenced one another.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
When real problems generate mathematics
Practical problems in insurance and risk management have given rise to important mathematical questions.
A first example comes from Scandinavia. Filip Lundberg, working as both an actuary and insurance executive, studied the evolution of an insurer’s surplus and the possibility of ruin in his 1903 doctoral work. Harald Cramér later developed these ideas into a central part of collective risk theory (Cramér 1969). The underlying business question is immediate: knowing the average cost of claims is not enough; an insurer must also survive their random timing and size.
A second example comes from the Netherlands. The North Sea flood of 1953 killed more than 1,800 people in the Netherlands and caused enormous damage. Dutch authorities then had to decide how strong sea defences should be when the relevant extreme water levels might occur only very rarely. David van Dantzig formulated the problem in explicitly statistical and economic terms, balancing the probability and consequences of flooding against the cost of stronger protection (Dantzig 1956).
This demand for extrapolation beyond ordinary observations remained a practical statistical problem. Decades later, Dutch extreme-value specialists, including Laurens de Haan, worked with public agencies on estimates of very rare sea levels used in coastal protection (Dillingh et al. 1993; Haan and Ronde 1998). The point is not that extreme-value theory was invented by the Dutch because of dykes. It is that a real problem of public risk management created a sustained demand for better extreme-value methods and brought mathematical statistics directly into engineering decisions.
Lundberg’s ruin theory and Dutch flood protection therefore illustrate the same broad mechanism: a practical problem comes first, and the mathematics becomes sharper because the decision requires it.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Insurance today
Insurance is now a layered international system. Individuals, households and firms buy cover from insurers; insurers diversify and use reinsurance; reinsurers distribute major risks across countries and capital providers; governments regulate solvency and market conduct and may intervene when losses are too concentrated for private balance sheets alone.
The range of insured risks has also widened enormously: property and marine insurance coexist with liability, motor, aviation, natural catastrophes, business interruption, cyber risk and many other lines. Yet the central questions are recognisable throughout the history of insurance: which risks should be pooled, how should they be priced, how dependent are the losses, how much capital is needed, and who ultimately bears the most extreme losses?

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
What to retain
The historical details are not examinable. The useful ideas are that insurance precedes probability theory, that pooling and diversification were practices before they were theorems, and that separating financing from risk transfer allowed insurance to become a specialised activity. Mathematics then entered insurance from several directions: demographic statistics and probability provided tools for pricing and aggregation, while practical problems such as insurer ruin and flood protection generated new mathematical work of their own.

title: The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
text:
Further reading
For a broad international history, see Borscheid and Haueter’s World Insurance (Borscheid and Haueter 2012). Leonard’s edited volume is useful on the origins and diffusion of marine insurance (Leonard 2016), while Pearson gives a detailed account of British fire insurance and industrialisation (Pearson 2004). Hald provides a technical history of probability and statistics before 1750 and from 1750 to 1930 (Hald 1990, 1998). For the Dutch flood case, Van Dantzig’s paper is unusually readable as an example of a real public-policy problem being translated into probabilistic and economic terms (Dantzig 1956).

title: Outline
text:
The course is organised into six chapters. The first two explore why insurance exists and how insurance contracts are designed. The middle chapters turn to pricing and aggregate-loss modelling, while the final two focus on risk measurement and dependence between risks.


The history of insurance and the role of mathematics
A brief historical introduction to insurance, from informal forms of mutual aid and early maritime risk sharing to the development of organised insurance markets. We will see how marine insurance gradually became distinct from credit and trade finance, how institutions such as Lloyd’s and fire insurers emerged, and how life assurance, reinsurance, social insurance and compulsory insurance developed over time. Particular attention will be paid to the interaction between practice and mathematics: insurance existed long before probability theory, but the development of probability, mortality tables, the law of large numbers and later actuarial and extreme-value methods progressively changed the way risks could be measured and managed. Conversely, some mathematical developments were themselves driven by concrete insurance and risk-management problems.
Microeconomics of insurance
Expected utility and risk aversion; the demand for insurance and its dependence on wealth; Mossin’s model; and the optimality of deductible contracts. We conclude with two central problems of insurance markets under asymmetric information: adverse selection and moral hazard.
